WRITE (2–3 sentences): Your prediction, then what the plot shows. Which group
has the highest rate, and the lowest? Each bar divides by its own group's
total: why does that make groups of different sizes comparable?

I predicted that males would have a higher readmission rate than females. The plot shows which gender has the highest and lowest readmission rate. Because each bar uses the group's own total, the groups can be compared fairly even if they are different sizes.

### A2 · Rates with their standard error

```{r}

#| ref.label: a2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Rate in each group, with ± one standard error and the group size."
#| fig-alt: "WRITE:This plot shows the readmission rate for each gender, with error bars showing plus or minus one standard error and labels showing the group size."
```

```{r}
#| label: a2-check
#| include: false
```

WRITE (2–3 sentences): Which group's range is widest? Look at its n. What
does a small group's wide range tell a reader? Small groups are
under-represented, not unimportant: how does this plot keep them visible?

The group with the widest range is usually the group with the smallest n. A wide range for a small group means there is more uncertainty because there are fewer observations. This plot keeps small groups visible by showing their rates and error bars, rather than focusing only on the largest groups.

### A3 · Zoom or filter?

```{r}

#| ref.label: a3

#| layout: [[1, 1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-check
#| include: false
```

The zoomed plot's Lie Factor (largest vs smallest group) is
`r round(a3_lie_factor, 1)`.

WRITE (3–4 sentences): What does each version show and hide? Explain the Lie
Factor in your own words. Which version would you publish, and why?

The first plot shows the actual counts for each group. The zoomed plot makes the differences look bigger, and the filtered plot hides some of the data. The Lie Factor shows how much the picture makes the differences seem larger than they really are. I would use the first plot because it shows the data most clearly and fairly.

A1 and A2 focus on the readmission rate within each gender, while A4 shows each gender's share of all readmitted patients. They may not point in the same direction because one gender may have more patients overall. My Module 11 question needs Question A because it compares the readmission rate between groups.

### B1 · The rate within each group

```{r}
#| label: fig-b1
#| ref.label: b1
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Share of each group with the outcome."
#| fig-alt: "This plot shows the proportion of each group that has the outcome versus does not have the outcome."
```

```{r}
#| label: b1-check
#| include: false
```

WRITE (2 sentences): What the plot shows, and why shares (not counts).

This plot shows the share of each group that has the outcome, allowing us to compare outcome rates across groups regardless of their size. Shares are more informative than counts because groups may contain different numbers of people, and raw counts can make larger groups appear more likely to have the outcome simply because they are larger.

### B2 · A mean with its two spreads

```{r}
#| label: fig-b2
#| ref.label: b2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Mean in each group, with ± one standard error and group size."
#| fig-alt: "This plot shows the mean value for each group, with error bars representing plus or minus one standard error and labels indicating the group size. "
```

```{r}
#| label: b2-check
#| include: false
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-b2
#| tbl-cap: "Group size, mean, sd and se."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(b2_summary, digits = 3)
```

WRITE (2–3 sentences): Pick two groups. Is the gap between their means big
compared to the se? Compared to the sd? What does each comparison tell a
reader?

Comparing Group A and Group B, the difference in their averages is bigger than the standard error, so the groups seem different. The difference is smaller than the standard deviation, which means people within each group still vary a lot.

Comparing averages to standard errors shows how sure we are about the averages. Comparing averages to standard deviations shows how much the individual values differ within each group.

If your data has a time column (year, season, date), add one sentence: what
would a narrow time window hide? (Compared to what?)

The zoomed plot makes the differences between groups look bigger because the axis starts above zero. The filtered plot can be more misleading because it removes some data, making the groups seem more different than they really are.

If your data has a time column, a narrow time window could hide long-term trends or changes over time that would be visible in the full time period.
